title: Masks
description: A mask changes two things simultaneously: the wearer becomes harder to read, and the wearer becomes less exposed. Both effects are real and usually operate in different directions for each person.
equipment: A mask. A simple masquerade mask works; a full face covering produces a stronger version of the same effect.

instructions.label: Solo first
instructions.content: Put on the mask and look at yourself in a mirror for two minutes. Notice what not being able to fully read your own face produces — whether the obscured identity feels distancing, freeing, or something else.

instructions.label: With a partner
instructions.content: One partner wears the mask throughout; the other doesn't. Engage as you normally would. As the masked person, notice what changes about how you act — whether partial anonymity feels freeing, alienating, or something harder to categorise. As the unmasked person, notice what not being able to read your partner's expression produces — whether they feel more or less present to you. After one round, swap.

explore: As the masked person: does obscuring your face change what you feel able to do or say?
Is the appeal the reduced exposure — less of yourself visible — or the persona the mask creates, or something else entirely?
As the unmasked person: does not being able to read your partner's expression change how you engage with them?
Does the mask make the other person feel more or less themselves — and which of those produces a stronger response in you?
why: Masks do two things at once: they reduce the wearer's exposure and they make the wearer harder to read. For the person wearing it, partial anonymity often changes what feels possible — the mask provides a layer between the self and the interaction that can function as permission. For the person seeing the masked face, the absence of readable expression creates a different quality of attention: you are looking at someone you know but cannot fully parse, and that gap in information produces its own kind of focus. The two effects typically operate asymmetrically — one person less exposed, one person less able to read — and the experience of that asymmetry is usually different from what both people anticipated.
